analysis.one_liner: Phases out ozone-destroying chemicals like CFCs and halons by 1997.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to phase out CFCs and halons by 1997 got one subcommittee hearing and died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have frozen production of ozone-destroying chemicals — CFCs and halons — at 1986 levels immediately, cut them to 80% by 1992, 50% by 1995, and banned them outright by 1997 except for essential medical uses. It required a 95% cut in total ozone-depleting potential by 1997, mandatory capture and recycling, warning labels, and import bans on chemicals and goods from countries without matching phase-out programs. It also directed the EPA to regulate chemicals that worsen human-caused climate change. The Senate referred it to committee, held one subcommittee hearing, and never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to the sun's ultraviolet rays. The bill's own findings cite evidence that CFC-driven ozone loss raises rates of skin cancer and cataracts, threatens food crops and marine resources, and that CFCs are also powerful greenhouse gases responsible for an estimated 15-25% of global warming [S3]. It protects people who own refrigerators, air conditioners, and cars by requiring those products to be built with fittings that capture the chemicals during repair and by barring the chemicals' release into the air [S3]. Consumers also get honest labeling telling them which products contain ozone-destroying substances [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone exposed to UV radiation and climate change

how_it_helps.text: Immediately froze production of CFCs and halons at 1986 levels, then cut them to 80% by 1992, 50% by 1995, and zero by 1997 — far faster than the international Montreal Protocol then in force, which the bill's findings said would still let atmospheric chlorine more than double [S3].

Required an overall 95% cut in ozone-depleting potential by 1997, closing the loophole that would otherwise let makers switch to a different chemical with a lower (but still real) ozone-depletion factor [S2].

Barred, starting in 1993, knowingly venting the regulated chemicals into the air, and required refrigerators and air conditioners to be built with service fittings so the chemicals can be captured during repair instead of escaping [S3].

Banned imports of the chemicals — and of products made with them — from any country without a phase-out program at least as strict as ours, so American producers could not simply be undercut by foreign suppliers [S2].
Required warning labels on containers and products stating that the contents 'harm public health and environment by destroying ozone in the upper atmosphere and by disrupting the climate' [S3].

Directed the EPA to write rules for any manufactured substance that worsens human-caused climate change, and gave the agency power to speed up phase-outs as new science came in, on petition from any member of the public [S2].

Gave citizens the right to sue violators and to sue the EPA if it fails to do its job, and set civil penalties up to $25,000 per day plus criminal penalties including up to two years in prison for knowing violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical companies that manufactured CFCs and halons, whose core products would be frozen, cut, and then banned outright by 1997 [S2]. Manufacturers of refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosols, foams, and fire-suppression equipment would bear the cost of redesigning products, installing recapture fittings, and switching to substitutes [S3]. Part of those costs would reach consumers as higher prices for appliances, car air conditioning, and imported goods made with the chemicals in countries without equivalent programs [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical makers, appliance manufacturers, and consumers

drawbacks.text: The phase-out deadlines were strict and mostly non-negotiable: production of priority-list chemicals had to hit zero by July 1997 with only a narrow medical exception, so if safe substitutes were not ready in time, prices for refrigeration, air conditioning, and fire suppression could spike [S2].

The bill provided no money to help workers in chemical plants or appliance factories transition, and no compensation for consumers who would pay more to replace or retrofit equipment built around the banned chemicals [S3].

The import ban extended beyond the raw chemicals to any product the EPA had reason to believe was 'manufactured with a process that uses' a listed chemical, with the burden on the importer to rebut the presumption — a rule that could snarl trade in ordinary goods [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — preventing skin cancer, cataracts, and crop damage from a thinning ozone layer, plus cutting one of the largest sources of greenhouse gases — are large, permanent, and shared by everyone. The costs are transitional and concentrated: a handful of chemical and equipment manufacturers would have to rebuild their product lines, and consumers would pay somewhat more for appliances and cooling in the meantime. The bill is carefully built to blunt the sharpest objections — it exempts essential medical uses, lets the President waive halon restrictions for national security, allows ten years to keep servicing existing household appliances, and lets the EPA speed up or adjust schedules as substitutes become available. An honest supporter would still acknowledge that the fixed 1997 deadline carried real risk of price shocks if substitute technologies lagged.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and was never reported to the full Senate before the two-year Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator John Chafee, a Republican, introduced the bill on March 2, 1989 together with Senator Max Baucus, a Democrat, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S1].
Ten senators signed on as cosponsors — 8 of the 55 Senate Democrats and 2 of the 45 Senate Republicans — giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from the start [S4].
On May 19, 1989, the Subcommittee on Environmental Protection held the bill's only hearings, printed as S.Hrg. 101-120 [S5].

No further action was ever taken: the full committee never voted to report the bill, the Senate never debated it, and no roll-call vote ever occurred before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Producers of CFCs and halons came out ahead: their chemicals stayed legal and in production while the bill sat in committee, and no senator ever had to cast a recorded vote on the phase-out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical makers who kept selling CFCs

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from birth — a Republican lead sponsor with 8 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors — but it died in committee without any floor vote, so the record shows no partisan split either way.

industries.note: The bill froze their production at 1986 levels immediately, cut it in steps, and banned it outright by 1997 except for essential medical uses — an existential hit to their core product lines. Their chemicals' profits came from products the bill's findings said were destroying the ozone shield that protects people from skin cancer.

They would have had to redesign products, install recapture fittings, and meet recycling and disposal rules — real compliance costs that reach consumers as higher prices. The bill also handed them a ten-year window to keep servicing existing household appliances after the 1997 ban, softening the blow.

industries.industry: Aerosol, foam, and fire-suppression product makers
industries.note: Their uses of the chemicals would be phased out on the same schedule, with a narrow escape hatch: the President could waive restrictions on halons, used in fire suppression, for national security for one year at a time.

The bill carves out an explicit exemption letting the EPA and FDA authorize continued production of banned chemicals for medical devices with no safe substitute, so their essential products keep working through and after the phase-out.
